claims.claim: Neuronal Nfasc is not an obligate component of early clusters (pre-nodes) in the CNS.
claims.source: This is consistent with the requirement of either the glial or the neuronal isoforms of the Nfasc gene for Nav recruitment to PNS nodes of Ranvier (Amor et al., 2017; Sherman et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015) but contrasts with the fact that neurofascins are neither required for the formation of early clusters in the CNS, nor is neuronal Nfasc an obligate component of these early clusters (pre-nodes) (Freeman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture are highly dynamic.
claims.source: Early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture are mobile and highly dynamic and can disintegrate or fuse with each other.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery (Figure 3) and time-lapse imaging showing movement and fusion (Figure 5, Figure 7).

claims.claim: Early clusters can disintegrate.
claims.source: Early clusters in PNS neurons in co-culture are mobile and highly dynamic and can disintegrate or fuse with each other.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing an early cluster fragmenting and disappearing (Figure 5C, Video 4).

claims.claim: Mobile early clusters can fuse with neighbouring heminodes.
claims.source: This view is supported by the ability of these mobile early clusters to fuse with neighbouring heminodes.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing an early cluster merging with a heminode (Figure 7B, Video 7).

claims.claim: Dynamic early clusters of nodal proteins in PNS nerves represent a Nfasc186-dependent developmental stage of node assembly during myelination that precedes heminode formation.
claims.source: We show that dynamic early clusters of nodal proteins in PNS nerves represent a Nfasc186-dependent developmental stage of node assembly during myelination that precedes heminode formation.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including temporal analysis, Nfasc dependency, and fusion with heminodes.

claims.claim: SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are targeted to the axonal plasma membrane during myelination by Schwann cells.
claims.source: First, we showed that SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are targeted appropriately to the axonal membrane during myelination (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging and immunostaining shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: Before myelin ensheathment, both SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP were diffusely distributed along the axolemma.
claims.source: Before myelin ensheathment, both proteins were diffusely distributed along the axolemma but became focally distributed at nodes after myelin ensheathment (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP became focally distributed at nodes after myelin ensheathment.
claims.source: Before myelin ensheathment, both proteins were diffusely distributed along the axolemma but became focally distributed at nodes after myelin ensheathment (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: Early clusters containing fluorescently tagged Nfasc186 or β1Nav are nodal protein complexes.
claims.source: Early clusters containing fluorescently tagged Nfasc186 or β1Nav are nodal protein complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining showing colocalization with nodal markers AnkG and βIV-spectrin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).

claims.claim: The transgenic fusion proteins SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are appropriate surrogate markers for detecting early clusters, heminodes, and nodes by live imaging.
claims.source: Hence, the transgenic fusion proteins are appropriate surrogate markers for detecting early clusters, heminodes, and nodes by live imaging.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these proteins localize correctly to nodal structures and colocalize with endogenous nodal markers.

claims.claim: β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters were barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons compared to Nfasc+/+ neurons.
claims.source: Although β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters assembled in Nfasc+/+ neurons, they were barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons (β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters/100 neurons, mean ± SEM: Nfasc+/+, 25.40 ± 5.60; Nfasc-/-, 0.21 ± 0.05; p = 0.0107, two-tailed unpaired student's t-test, n = 3 independent cultures).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative comparison showing statistically significant difference (p = 0.0107).

claims.claim: Glial neurofascin isoform Nfasc155 plays no part in early cluster formation.
claims.source: These co-cultures are not completely neurofascin-null since WT Schwann cells express the glial neurofascin isoform, Nfasc155. However, this isoform clearly plays no part in early cluster formation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early clusters do not form in Nfasc-/- neurons even though WT Schwann cells expressing Nfasc155 are present.

claims.claim: Neuronal neurofascin is necessary for the assembly of early clusters.
claims.source: Hence, neuronal neurofascin is not only important in node formation but also necessary for the assembly of early clusters.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the absence of early clusters in Nfasc-/- neurons.

claims.claim: Schwann cells are required for early cluster formation.
claims.source: Therefore, we wished to explore the dependency of early cluster formation on Schwann cells. We showed that not only were Schwann cells required for early cluster formation but also they must be induced to myelinate in the presence of ascorbic acid (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing early clusters do not form without Schwann cells (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: Schwann cells must be induced to myelinate in the presence of ascorbic acid for early cluster formation.
claims.source: Therefore, we wished to explore the dependency of early cluster formation on Schwann cells. We showed that not only were Schwann cells required for early cluster formation but also they must be induced to myelinate in the presence of ascorbic acid (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments comparing conditions with and without myelinating medium (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: Laminin stimulates myelination and enhanced early cluster formation.
claims.source: Laminin, a component of matrigel, stimulates myelination and enhanced early cluster formation (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing early cluster formation in matrigel-coated versus collagen-coated chambers (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: The presence of Schwann cells alone is not sufficient for early cluster formation.
claims.source: Hence, the presence of Schwann cells alone is not sufficient for early cluster formation, but they must also be myelinating.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing early clusters do not form when Schwann cells are present but not induced to myelinate (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: Schwann cell microvillar markers including pERM, dystrophin isoform 116 (Dp116), and radixin are not detectable at early clusters.
claims.source: However, although gliomedin is also found in the microvilli at the extremities of myelinating Schwann cells (Eshed et al., 2005), no other Schwann cell microvillar markers, including pERM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), dystrophin isoform 116 (Dp116), and radixin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), were detectable at early clusters, despite being strongly enriched at heminodes and nodes.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli.
claims.source: Thus, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of microvillar markers at early clusters.

claims.claim: CLEM confirmed the close contact between Schwann cells and axons at early clusters.
claims.source: CLEM confirmed the close contact between Schwann cells and axons at early clusters (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by correlative light and electron microscopy shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CLEM did not reveal any axo-glial ultrastructural specialisations at early clusters that might contribute to their formation.
claims.source: These results underscored the close physical proximity of Schwann cells and axonal early clusters but did not reveal any axo-glial ultrastructural specialisations that might contribute to their formation.
claims.evidence: This is based on examination of serial EM sections shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Mature nodes are very stable structures.
claims.source: Mature nodes are very stable structures (Zonta et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Zonta et al., 2011 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Heminodes and nascent nodes can exchange proteins with an axolemmal pool.
claims.source: In contrast, heminodes and nascent nodes can exchange proteins with an axolemmal pool (Zhang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2020, and confirmed by the authors' FRAP experiments.

claims.claim: SEP-Nfasc186 expressed on the axons of neurons cultured without Schwann cells was highly mobile.
claims.source: SEP-Nfasc186 expressed on the axons of neurons cultured without Schwann cells was highly mobile (Figure 3A–C; Video 1), which was consistent with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2012; Ghosh et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A-C and Video 1.

claims.claim: SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters was less mobile than on unmyelinated axons, but the recovery of their fluorescence intensity levels indicated that they are highly dynamic structures.
claims.source: SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters was less mobile, but the recovery of their fluorescence intensity levels indicated that they are highly dynamic structures, whereas nodal SEP-Nfasc186 was relatively immobile (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A-C.

claims.claim: Nodal SEP-Nfasc186 was relatively immobile.
claims.source: SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters was less mobile, but the recovery of their fluorescence intensity levels indicated that they are highly dynamic structures, whereas nodal SEP-Nfasc186 was relatively immobile (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing minimal fluorescence recovery at nodes (Figure 3A-C).

claims.claim: SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes displayed mobilities intermediate between early clusters and nodes.
claims.source: SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes displayed mobilities intermediate between early clusters and nodes (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A-C.

claims.claim: The mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 at nodal clusters gradually declines as it acquires more mature features.
claims.source: Thus, the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 at nodal clusters gradually declines as it acquires more mature features.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mobility decreases from unmyelinated axons to early clusters to heminodes to nodes.

claims.claim: Heminodes are dynamic structures that can rapidly exchange full-length Nfasc186 with the axonal pool.
claims.source: Our observation that heminodes are dynamic structures is particularly intriguing and represents the first direct demonstration that, unlike nodes, they can rapidly exchange full-length Nfasc186 with the axonal pool.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery at heminodes (Figure 3).

claims.claim: FLIP completely prevented FRAP at early clusters.
claims.source: FLIP completely prevented FRAP at early clusters (Figure 3D,E and G; Video 2), indicating that SEP-Nfasc186 fluorescence recovery at these structures is exclusively via lateral diffusion from the axonal surface pool.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3D, E, G and Video 2.

claims.claim: SEP-Nfasc186 fluorescence recovery at early clusters is exclusively via lateral diffusion from the axonal surface pool.
claims.source: FLIP completely prevented FRAP at early clusters (Figure 3D,E and G; Video 2), indicating that SEP-Nfasc186 fluorescence recovery at these structures is exclusively via lateral diffusion from the axonal surface pool.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments showing no recovery when lateral diffusion is blocked (Figure 3D, E, G).

claims.claim: Fluorescence recovery at heminodes is predominantly mediated by the pool of SEP-Nfasc186 on the flanking unmyelinated axon.
claims.source: Interestingly, FRAP/FLIP showed that the same mode of fluorescence recovery applies to heminodes and that this recovery is predominantly mediated by the pool of SEP-Nfasc186 on the flanking unmyelinated axon (Figure 3D,F and G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by asymmetric FLIP experiments showing recovery is prevented when the unmyelinated side is photobleached (Figure 3D, F, G).

claims.claim: Neither the number nor the speed of mobile axonal β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles is affected by FLIP.
claims.source: We found that neither the number nor the speed of mobile axonal β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles is affected by FLIP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C), indicating that FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport of this membrane protein.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of vesicle movement before and after FLIP shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claims.claim: FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport of β1Nav-EGFP.
claims.source: We found that neither the number nor the speed of mobile axonal β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles is affected by FLIP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C), indicating that FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport of this membrane protein.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vesicle movement is unchanged after FLIP.

claims.claim: β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile.
claims.source: Thus, like SEP-Nfasc186, β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile, but its turnover rate is considerably slower.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery at β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).

claims.claim: The turnover rate of β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is considerably slower than SEP-Nfasc186.
claims.source: Thus, like SEP-Nfasc186, β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile, but its turnover rate is considerably slower.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that β1Nav-EGFP requires 4 hours to recover to levels comparable to SEP-Nfasc186.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment resulted in a marked reduction in the mobility of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles in DRG axons.
claims.source: Nocodazole treatment resulted in a marked reduction in the mobility of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles in DRG axons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D) but had no effect on the recovery of β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters after photobleaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of vesicle movement shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claims.claim: Nocodazole treatment had no effect on the recovery of β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters after photobleaching.
claims.source: Nocodazole treatment resulted in a marked reduction in the mobility of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicles in DRG axons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D) but had no effect on the recovery of β1Nav-EGFP+ early clusters after photobleaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments in the presence of nocodazole shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and F.

claims.claim: β1Nav-EGFP fluorescence in early clusters recovers by lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane.
claims.source: This indicated that, like Nfasc186, β1Nav-EGFP fluorescence in early clusters recovers by lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nocodazole, which blocks vesicular transport, does not affect fluorescence recovery at early clusters.

claims.claim: Fluorescence recovery of SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters is unaffected in Caspr-null DRG axons from Cntnap1-/- mice.
claims.source: Since distinct axo-glial specialisations are not apparent at the ultrastructural level in their vicinity (Figure 2C), we predicted that fluorescence recovery of SEP-Nfasc186 in early clusters would be unaffected in Caspr-null DRG axons from Cntnap1-/- mice (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing similar recovery in Cntnap1+/+ and Cntnap1-/- early clusters (Figure 4A, B, C).

claims.claim: The absence of Caspr did not influence the assembly of early clusters.
claims.source: Furthermore, the absence of Caspr, and hence of paranodal axo-glial junctions (Bhat et al., 2001), did not influence the assembly of early clusters (SEP-Nfasc186+ early clusters/100 neurons; mean ± SEM: Cntnap1+/+, 90.2 ± 28.3; Cntnap1-/-, 90.9 ± 15.0; p = 0.9838; two-tailed paired student's t-test; n = 3 independent cultures).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification showing no significant difference in early cluster numbers between Cntnap1+/+ and Cntnap1-/- (p = 0.9838).

claims.claim: Loss of paranodal axo-glial junctions had no significant effect on the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes.
claims.source: Perhaps surprisingly, loss of paranodal axo-glial junctions had no significant effect on the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes, but, and consistent with earlier reports (Zhang et al., 2020), junctional disruption significantly increased protein mobility at mature nodes (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4A, B, C.

claims.claim: Junctional disruption significantly increased protein mobility at mature nodes.
claims.source: Perhaps surprisingly, loss of paranodal axo-glial junctions had no significant effect on the mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 in heminodes, but, and consistent with earlier reports (Zhang et al., 2020), junctional disruption significantly increased protein mobility at mature nodes (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing increased recovery at Cntnap1-/- nodes compared to WT nodes (Figure 4A, B, C).

claims.claim: The insensitivity of SEP-Nfasc186 mobility in heminodes to junctional disruption reflects the dominant contribution of fluorescence recovery of lateral diffusion from the unmyelinated side that lacks an axo-glial junction.
claims.source: The insensitivity of SEP-Nfasc186 mobility in heminodes to junctional disruption presumably reflects the dominant contribution of fluorescence recovery of lateral diffusion from the unmyelinated side that lacks an axo-glial junction (Figure 3D,F and G).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetric FLIP experiments showing recovery is predominantly from the unmyelinated side.

claims.claim: The ability of SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes to partially recover after photobleaching was completely ablated when fluorescence recovery by lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 was impeded by performing FRAP/FLIP.
claims.source: We observed that the ability of SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes to partially recover after photobleaching was completely ablated when fluorescence recovery by lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 was impeded by performing FRAP/FLIP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP/FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: FLIP alone did not affect the fluorescence intensity of SEP-Nfasc186+/WT nodes.
claims.source: Furthermore, while FLIP alone did not affect the fluorescence intensity of SEP-Nfasc186+/WT nodes, it resulted in significant loss of fluorescence at SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claims.claim: FLIP resulted in significant loss of fluorescence at SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes.
claims.source: Furthermore, while FLIP alone did not affect the fluorescence intensity of SEP-Nfasc186+/WT nodes, it resulted in significant loss of fluorescence at SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by FLIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claims.claim: Paranodal axo-glial junctions act as diffusion barriers that stabilize nodes.
claims.source: Using FRAP and FRAP/FLIP, we now provide direct evidence for this. We observed that the ability of SEP-Nfasc186+/Caspr-null nodes to partially recover after photobleaching was completely ablated when fluorescence recovery by lateral diffusion of SEP-Nfasc186 was impeded by performing FRAP/FLIP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that in the absence of paranodal junctions, nodes can exchange proteins with the axonal pool, and this exchange is blocked by FLIP.

claims.claim: The formation of axo-glial junctions has a profound effect on the dynamic properties of mature nodal assemblies.
claims.source: Collectively, these results support the view that early clusters are highly dynamic structures untrammelled by axo-glial interactions and further demonstrate that the formation of axo-glial junctions has a profound effect on the dynamic properties of mature nodal assemblies.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nodes without paranodal junctions are more dynamic than WT nodes.

claims.claim: The vast majority of early clusters remained clearly visible over an 18-hr time-lapse imaging period.
claims.source: The vast majority of early clusters remained clearly visible over an 18-hr time-lapse imaging period and appeared to migrate along the axon (Figure 5A; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and Video 3.

claims.claim: Early clusters appeared to migrate along the axon.
claims.source: The vast majority of early clusters remained clearly visible over an 18-hr time-lapse imaging period and appeared to migrate along the axon (Figure 5A; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5A and Video 3.

claims.claim: The perceived movement of early clusters could not be explained by axonal extension.
claims.source: When the position of early clusters was recorded in relation to immobile landmarks, such as axonal branching points or points of intersection with other axons, it became apparent that the perceived movement of early clusters could not be explained by axonal extension (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by tracking early clusters relative to fixed landmarks shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: When multiple early clusters were present on the same axonal segment, they almost invariably moved synchronously in the same direction and at the same speed.
claims.source: Interestingly, when multiple early clusters were present on the same axonal segment, they almost invariably moved synchronously in the same direction and at the same speed (Figure 5D; Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 5D and Video 5.

claims.claim: Treatment with latrunculin A strongly impaired the movement of early clusters.
claims.source: Treatment with latrunculin A strongly impaired the movement of early clusters, significantly reducing both the percentage and the speed of early clusters that were mobile (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B and D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of early cluster movement in the presence of latrunculin A shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Latrunculin A effectively disrupted the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: Latrunculin A effectively disrupted the actin cytoskeleton, as evidenced by the dramatic reduction in the intensity of phalloidin staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Blebbistatin significantly reduced the speed of mobile early clusters.
claims.source: Blebbistatin significantly reduced the speed of mobile early clusters, indicating that myosin II contributes to early cluster migration along axons (mean ± SEM: dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 0.99 ± 0.09 μm/s; blebbistatin, 0.70 ± 0.03, p = 0.0233, two-tailed paired student's t-test, n = 4 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification showing statistically significant reduction in speed (p = 0.0233).

claims.claim: Myosin II contributes to early cluster migration along axons.
claims.source: Blebbistatin significantly reduced the speed of mobile early clusters, indicating that myosin II contributes to early cluster migration along axons (mean ± SEM: dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 0.99 ± 0.09 μm/s; blebbistatin, 0.70 ± 0.03, p = 0.0233, two-tailed paired student's t-test, n = 4 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blebbistatin, a myosin II inhibitor, reduces early cluster speed.

claims.claim: Node-like clusters were consistently observed 5 days after the induction of myelination, a stage at which no heminodes or nodes were detectable.
claims.source: We consistently observed node-like clusters 5 days after the induction of myelination, a stage at which no heminodes or nodes were detectable (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The number of early clusters consistently peaked at a time corresponding to the first appearance of heminodes and nodes.
claims.source: The number of early clusters consistently peaked at a time corresponding to the first appearance of heminodes and nodes, and then steadily declined to almost zero by 40 days after the induction of myelination (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification over time shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The number of early clusters steadily declined to almost zero by 40 days after the induction of myelination.
claims.source: The number of early clusters consistently peaked at a time corresponding to the first appearance of heminodes and nodes, and then steadily declined to almost zero by 40 days after the induction of myelination (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification over time shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The appearance of heminodes and nodes in the distal axonal compartment was consistently delayed compared to the somal compartment.
claims.source: Although the appearance of heminodes and nodes in the distal axonal compartment was consistently delayed compared to the somal compartment (Figure 6A), we also found, consistent with what we had observed in the somal compartment, that the initiation of assembly of early clusters preceded heminode and node formation in the axonal compartment (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in both compartments shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The initiation of assembly of early clusters preceded heminode and node formation in the axonal compartment.
claims.source: Although the appearance of heminodes and nodes in the distal axonal compartment was consistently delayed compared to the somal compartment (Figure 6A), we also found, consistent with what we had observed in the somal compartment, that the initiation of assembly of early clusters preceded heminode and node formation in the axonal compartment (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in the axonal compartment shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Assembly of early clusters proceeds sequentially in a somal-to-distal direction in vitro.
claims.source: This indicates that, like heminodes and nodes, assembly of early clusters proceeds sequentially in a somal-to-distal direction in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early clusters appear earlier in the somal compartment than in the distal axonal compartment.

claims.claim: The sequential appearance of early clusters, followed by heminodes, followed by nodes, observed in co-cultures, was also observed in vivo.
claims.source: The sequential appearance of early clusters, followed by heminodes, followed by nodes, observed in co-cultures, was also observed in vivo (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in sciatic nerves at P1, P3, and P5 shown in Figure 6B and C.

claims.claim: Early cluster assembly is a temporally regulated developmental stage of PNS myelination both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: Taken together, our data show that early cluster assembly is a temporally regulated developmental stage of PNS myelination both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis showing early clusters appear first, peak, and then decline as heminodes and nodes increase, both in culture and in vivo.

claims.claim: The vast majority of early clusters were mobile (84.2 ± 2.2%).
claims.source: We found that the vast majority of early clusters were mobile (% of mobile early clusters, mean ± SEM, 84.2 ± 2.2, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture) and progressed along the axon at an average speed of 0.88 ± 0.03 µm/h (mean ± SEM, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of early cluster movement.

claims.claim: Early clusters progressed along the axon at an average speed of 0.88 ± 0.03 µm/h.
claims.source: We found that the vast majority of early clusters were mobile (% of mobile early clusters, mean ± SEM, 84.2 ± 2.2, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture) and progressed along the axon at an average speed of 0.88 ± 0.03 µm/h (mean ± SEM, n = 3 independent cultures, ≥10 axons per culture).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of early cluster movement speed.

claims.claim: Without exception, mobile early clusters advanced retrogradely towards the nearest heminode.
claims.source: Without exception, mobile early clusters advanced retrogradely towards the nearest heminode, while no early clusters moved in the anterograde direction.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of early cluster movement direction relative to heminodes.

claims.claim: No early clusters moved in the anterograde direction.
claims.source: Without exception, mobile early clusters advanced retrogradely towards the nearest heminode, while no early clusters moved in the anterograde direction.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of early cluster movement direction.

claims.claim: Neither the directionality nor the speed of early clusters was influenced by their distance from the nearest myelinated segment.
claims.source: Neither the directionality nor the speed of early clusters was influenced by their distance from the nearest myelinated segment (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated by the authors based on their analysis.

claims.claim: Early clusters can migrate towards and contribute to heminode formation.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings indicate that early clusters can migrate towards and contribute to heminode formation (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing early clusters fusing with heminodes (Figure 7B) and the model in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Early clusters are the earliest nodal complexes in the pathway to the assembly of the node of Ranvier in culture and in vivo.
claims.source: Hence, they are the earliest nodal complexes in the pathway to the assembly of the node of Ranvier in culture and in vivo (Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis and fusion observations, and supported by citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Disruption of nodal complex assembly is incompatible with normal nervous system development and results in perinatal mortality in rodent models.
claims.source: Disruption of nodal complex assembly is incompatible with normal nervous system development and results in perinatal mortality in rodent models and severe neurodevelopmental defects in humans (Sherman et al., 2005; Maluenda et al., 2016; Wambach et al., 2017; Laquérriere et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2017; Mehta et al., 2017; Conant et al., 2018; Nizon et al., 2017; Monfrini et al., 2019; Smigiel et al., 2018; SYNAPS Study Group et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Disruption of nodal complex assembly results in severe neurodevelopmental defects in humans.
claims.source: Disruption of nodal complex assembly is incompatible with normal nervous system development and results in perinatal mortality in rodent models and severe neurodevelopmental defects in humans (Sherman et al., 2005; Maluenda et al., 2016; Wambach et al., 2017; Laquérriere et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2017; Mehta et al., 2017; Conant et al., 2018; Nizon et al., 2017; Monfrini et al., 2019; Smigiel et al., 2018; SYNAPS Study Group et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Early clusters of nodal protein complexes represent the earliest Nav clustering event in the PNS.

claims.source: In conclusion, we describe a new aspect of the diverse redundant mechanisms that appears to be a characteristic of a critical stage in the development of the vertebrate nervous system, namely the assembly of nodes of Ranvier. We have presented evidence that early clusters of nodal protein complexes represent the earliest Nav clustering event in the PNS, that their assembly is at an early developmental stage of myelination, and that they can actively contribute to the assembly of nodes of Ranvier.

results.result: Early clusters of nodal proteins appear before heminodes and nodes during peripheral nerve myelination, representing the earliest stage of node assembly. Temporal quantification in vitro and in vivo demonstrates that early clusters peak at 5-10 days after myelination induction, preceding the appearance of heminodes and nodes, and then decline as more mature structures form.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C12, C19, C21, C86-C93, C154, and C155 collectively demonstrate through temporal quantification (Figure 6) that early clusters appear first, peak when heminodes/nodes begin forming, then decline. This temporal relationship is shown both in vitro (microfluidic cultures) and in vivo (P1, P3, P5 sciatic nerves), with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The sequential appearance in somal-to-distal direction further supports developmental progression.

results.result: Formation of early clusters in the PNS requires neuronal neurofascin 186 (Nfasc186), distinguishing them from CNS early clusters which do not require neurofascins. Early clusters are barely detectable in Nfasc-/- neurons (0.21±0.05 vs 25.40±5.60 per 100 neurons in WT, p=0.0107), while glial Nfasc155 plays no role.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C24, C39-C41, and C132 are well-supported by experiments comparing Nfasc+/+ and Nfasc-/- neurons co-cultured with WT Schwann cells. The statistically significant reduction (p=0.0107, n=3) demonstrates Nfasc186 dependency. The presence of glial Nfasc155 without rescue confirms isoform specificity. Citation to Freeman et al. 2015 appropriately contrasts with CNS findings.

results.result: Nodal proteins in early clusters are dynamically recruited exclusively by lateral diffusion in the axonal membrane, not by direct vesicular delivery. FRAP experiments show fluorescence recovery at early clusters, which is completely prevented by FLIP (blocking lateral diffusion), demonstrating that protein recruitment occurs via surface diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C23, C53, C58, C59, C133, and C134 are strongly supported by FRAP and FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 3). The complete prevention of recovery by FLIP directly demonstrates lateral diffusion as the exclusive mechanism. Controls showing FLIP does not affect vesicle transport (C61-C62) and nocodazole experiments with β1Nav-EGFP (C65-C67) further validate this conclusion.

results.result: Early clusters are mobile and can fuse with each other and with heminodes, actively contributing to node assembly. Time-lapse imaging demonstrates early clusters moving retrogradely toward heminodes at 0.88±0.03 μm/h, with 84.2±2.2% being mobile, and directly shows fusion events.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C32, C99, and C156 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figures 5, 7, Videos 3-7) showing early cluster movement, fusion between early clusters, and fusion with heminodes. Quantification of movement speed and directionality (C94-C97) provides statistical support. The observation that all mobile early clusters move retrogradely toward heminodes strengthens the developmental relationship.

results.result: Early cluster formation requires the presence of myelinating Schwann cells. Schwann cells must be induced to myelinate with ascorbic acid; their presence alone without myelination induction is insufficient for early cluster formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C42, C43, and C45 are supported by experiments (Figure 2A) comparing conditions with/without Schwann cells and with/without myelinating medium. The requirement for both Schwann cells AND myelination induction is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls and statistical significance (p<0.01, p<0.0001).

results.result: Unlike heminodes, early clusters are not contacted by Schwann cell microvilli and lack axo-glial ultrastructural specializations. Immunostaining shows absence of microvillar markers (pERM, Dp116, radixin) at early clusters, and CLEM reveals close Schwann cell proximity without specialized junctions.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C46-C49, and C148 are well-supported by immunostaining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing absence of microvillar markers and CLEM (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) showing no ultrastructural specializations. The contrast with heminodes/nodes where these markers are present strengthens the conclusion. Serial EM sections provide thorough structural analysis.

results.result: Early cluster formation is independent of paranodal axo-glial junctions. Assembly of early clusters is unaffected in Caspr-null neurons (90.2±28.3 vs 90.9±15.0 per 100 neurons, p=0.9838), and fluorescence recovery at early clusters shows no difference between Cntnap1+/+ and Cntnap1-/- conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C68, and C69 are supported by experiments in Caspr-null (Cntnap1-/-) neurons showing no effect on early cluster assembly (quantification with p=0.9838) or dynamics (FRAP experiments, Figure 4). This independence from paranodal junctions distinguishes early clusters from mature nodes and is consistent with the absence of axo-glial specializations.

results.result: The mobility of SEP-Nfasc186 at nodal structures gradually declines during maturation. FRAP experiments show highest mobility on unmyelinated axons, intermediate mobility at early clusters and heminodes, and minimal mobility at mature nodes, indicating progressive stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by systematic FRAP experiments (Figure 3A-C) comparing all four conditions with appropriate quantification. The gradient of mobility (unmyelinated > early clusters > heminodes > nodes) is clearly demonstrated and consistent with progressive maturation. Confirmation in ex vivo triangularis sterni preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) strengthens the finding.

results.result: Heminodes are dynamic structures that rapidly exchange full-length Nfasc186 with the axonal pool, predominantly via lateral diffusion from the flanking unmyelinated axon. Asymmetric FRAP/FLIP experiments demonstrate that recovery is prevented when the unmyelinated side is photobleached.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C60, C140, and C141 are supported by FRAP and asymmetric FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 3D, F, G) showing fluorescence recovery at heminodes and demonstrating the predominant contribution from the unmyelinated side. This represents the first direct demonstration of full-length Nfasc186 exchange at heminodes, as stated by the authors.

results.result: Paranodal axo-glial junctions act as diffusion barriers that stabilize mature nodes. Loss of junctions in Caspr-null mice significantly increases protein mobility at nodes but not at heminodes or early clusters. FRAP/FLIP experiments directly demonstrate that nodes without junctions can exchange proteins with the axonal pool via lateral diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C71, C73-C76, C143, and C144 are strongly supported by FRAP experiments in Caspr-null mice (Figure 4) showing increased nodal mobility, and FRAP/FLIP experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) demonstrating that recovery at Caspr-null nodes is prevented by blocking lateral diffusion. FLIP alone causing fluorescence loss at Caspr-null but not WT nodes provides direct evidence for the barrier function.

results.result: Early clusters are mobile along axons, with 84.2±2.2% showing movement at an average speed of 0.88±0.03 μm/h. Movement is not explained by axonal extension (tracked relative to fixed landmarks), and multiple early clusters on the same axon move synchronously. All mobile early clusters move retrogradely toward the nearest heminode.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 and C94-C97 are supported by extensive time-lapse imaging (Figure 5, Videos 3-5) with quantification of mobility percentage and speed. Tracking relative to immobile landmarks (C80) rules out axonal extension. The exclusive retrograde movement toward heminodes (C96-C97) is particularly compelling evidence for developmental contribution to node formation.

results.result: Early cluster movement is actin-dependent and involves myosin II. Latrunculin A treatment significantly reduces both the percentage and speed of mobile early clusters, while blebbistatin (myosin II inhibitor) significantly reduces movement speed (0.70±0.03 vs 0.99±0.09 μm/s, p=0.0233).
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) with latrunculin A and blebbistatin. Effective actin disruption is confirmed by phalloidin staining (C83). Statistical significance for blebbistatin effect (p=0.0233, n=4) supports myosin II involvement. However, the authors cannot distinguish between axonal and Schwann cell contributions to motility.

results.result: β1Nav-EGFP in early clusters is mobile and recovers by lateral diffusion, though with slower turnover than SEP-Nfasc186 (requiring 4 hours vs 15 minutes). Nocodazole treatment blocks vesicle transport but does not affect fluorescence recovery at early clusters, demonstrating lateral diffusion as the recruitment mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by FRAP experiments with β1Nav-EGFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing recovery over 4 hours, and nocodazole experiments demonstrating that blocking microtubule-based transport does not prevent recovery. The slower turnover compared to Nfasc186 is appropriately noted. Controls showing nocodazole effectively blocks vesicle movement strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The transgenic fusion proteins SEP-Nfasc186 and β1Nav-EGFP are appropriately targeted to the axonal membrane and serve as valid surrogate markers for nodal structures. Both proteins are diffusely distributed before myelination and become focally concentrated at nodes after myelination, colocalizing with endogenous nodal markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by live imaging and immunostaining (Figure 1) showing proper localization and colocalization with AnkG and βIV-spectrin. The validation that early clusters in transgenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) show similar percentages to WT mice (81.7-86.7% at P1) confirms the transgenes do not artifactually alter early cluster formation.

results.result: FLIP does not affect microtubule-based vesicle transport. Analysis of β1Nav-EGFP+ vesicle movement before and after FRAP/FLIP shows no change in number or speed of mobile vesicles, validating that FLIP specifically blocks lateral diffusion without causing photodamage to the cytoskeleton.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C62 are supported by control experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) quantifying vesicle movement before and after FLIP. This important control validates the FRAP/FLIP methodology and rules out non-specific effects of photobleaching on cellular transport machinery.

results.result: Background claims establishing that voltage-gated sodium channels cluster at nodes of Ranvier for rapid conduction, that node assembly is thought to be initiated at heminodes with fusion leading to nodes, and that neurofascin proteins are essential for node formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C5, and C13 represent well-established background knowledge supported by extensive prior research and citations. These provide the necessary context for the study's findings but are not novel results of this work.

results.result: Prior observations of nodal protein complexes lacking flanking Schwann cells or myelin have been reported in various systems, and these structures can enhance conduction velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 accurately cite prior literature (Eshed-Eisenbach et al. 2020, Lambert et al. 1997, Freeman et al. 2015) establishing that similar structures have been observed before. These citations appropriately contextualize the current study's focus on characterizing these structures.

results.result: Background claims about redundant mechanisms of node assembly in PNS and CNS, including roles of Nfasc isoforms, gliomedin, paranodal junctions, and extracellular matrix proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 and C103-C116 accurately represent established knowledge from cited literature about node assembly mechanisms. These provide important context for understanding the significance of early clusters as an additional mechanism, but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Laminin stimulates myelination and enhances early cluster formation, as demonstrated by comparing matrigel-coated versus collagen-coated chambers.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2A comparing different coating conditions. However, this is a methodological observation rather than a mechanistic finding about early cluster biology.

results.result: Background claims that mature nodes are very stable structures while heminodes and nascent nodes can exchange proteins with an axolemmal pool.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 cite prior literature (Zonta et al. 2011, Zhang et al. 2012, 2020) and are confirmed by the authors' FRAP experiments. These establish the context for comparing early cluster dynamics to other nodal structures.

results.result: The insensitivity of SEP-Nfasc186 mobility in heminodes to junctional disruption reflects the dominant contribution of lateral diffusion from the unmyelinated side that lacks an axo-glial junction.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is a reasonable inference from the asymmetric FLIP experiments (C60) showing recovery predominantly from the unmyelinated side. Since heminodes have only one paranodal junction, loss of that junction would not affect recovery from the unmyelinated side.

results.result: Like heminodes, early cluster assembly depends on the interaction between Schwann cell-secreted gliomedin and neuronal Nfasc186, and they are not essential for node formation since nodes still form in the absence of gliomedin.
results.evaluation: Claims C117 and C118 are supported by the demonstrated Nfasc186 requirement (C24, C39-C41) and citation to Feinberg et al. 2010 showing nodes form without gliomedin. The gliomedin dependency is inferred from prior knowledge about its role at heminodes and its presence at early clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

results.result: The clustering activity of gliomedin is negatively regulated by proteolytic cleavage by BMP1/Tolloid-like proteases, and inhibition of these proteases enhances early cluster formation without affecting myelination or node assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C119 and C120 cite Eshed-Eisenbach et al. 2020 and provide context for understanding regulation of early cluster formation. These are not findings of the current study but relevant prior work.

results.result: Early cluster assembly is restricted to large calibre NF200-positive axons that typically become myelinated in vivo, and early clusters do not assemble on unmyelinated C-type fibers in Remak bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by the authors' observations (stated as "data not shown" for C121) and citation to Eshed-Eisenbach et al. 2020 for C123. This specificity for myelinated axon types is consistent with early clusters being developmental intermediates in node formation.

results.result: CNS and PNS early clusters share many similarities including timing, molecular composition, glial factor dependence, persistence after myelination, and enhancement of conduction velocity. It is possible they share similar developmental roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C131 appropriately cite extensive prior literature on CNS early clusters and draw parallels to the PNS structures characterized in this study. Claim C131 is appropriately cautious speculation ("it is possible") based on the documented similarities.

results.result: Background claims about Nav and Nfasc186 delivery to nodes, including that Nav α and β subunits can be independently delivered and might follow different routes.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139 cite prior literature and provide context for the finding that β1Nav-EGFP is recruited by lateral diffusion. Claim C139 is appropriate speculation based on the observation that the subunits can be independently delivered (C137-C138).

results.result: The ability of both early clusters and heminodes to exchange Nfasc186 with the unmyelinated axon is consistent with their ability to merge.
results.evaluation: Claim C142 is a reasonable inference connecting the dynamic properties demonstrated by FRAP (C53, C57, C60) with the observed fusion events (C10, C32). The shared mechanism of lateral diffusion provides a plausible basis for fusion.

results.result: The molecular interactions between Nfasc186 and other nodal proteins are not intrinsically different between mature nodes and early clusters but are modulated by axo-glial junctions. In the absence of junctions, Nfasc186 could potentially diffuse through internodal regions and exchange between adjacent nodes.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is a reasonable inference from the FRAP data in Caspr-null mice showing nodes behave more like early clusters. However, claims C146 and C147 are speculation ("could, conceivably") that goes beyond the data. While plausible based on the demonstrated lateral diffusion, actual internodal diffusion or node-to-node exchange was not directly observed.

results.result: Schwann cell microvilli emerge at early stages of Schwann cell maturation before myelin ensheathment, and their absence at early clusters likely contributes to the dynamic properties of early clusters.
results.evaluation: Claim C149 cites Gatto et al. 2003 appropriately. Claim C150 is reasonable inference from the structural differences (C22, C46-C47, C148) and dynamic properties (C7, C29, C53), though the causal relationship is not directly tested.

results.result: This is the first documented example of long-range movement of membrane-bound protein complexes along the axon, excluding heminodes.
results.evaluation: Claim C151 is stated based on the authors' knowledge of the literature ("To our knowledge"). While the observation of early cluster movement is well-documented (C78-C81, C94-C97), the claim of being "first" cannot be fully verified without comprehensive literature review. The exclusion of heminodes is appropriate since their movement has been observed.

results.result: Schwann cells contacting early clusters appear to migrate along the axon at similar rates to early clusters, and might be responsible for early cluster motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C152 and C153 are based on observations stated as "data not shown" and explicitly presented as hypothesis ("we hypothesise"). While the actin-dependence (C82-C85) is consistent with Schwann cell involvement, the mechanism remains unresolved. The authors appropriately acknowledge they "cannot exclude an axon-based mechanism."

results.result: Neither the directionality nor the speed of early clusters was influenced by their distance from the nearest myelinated segment.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is stated as "data not shown," making it impossible to evaluate the quality of the analysis or statistical support. While this observation would be consistent with the overall findings, it cannot be properly assessed without seeing the data.

results.result: Early clusters contribute to the development of nodes in peripheral axons and represent a Nfasc186-dependent developmental stage of node assembly that precedes heminode formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C33, and C100 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple lines of evidence: temporal precedence (C4, C12, C86-C93), Nfasc186 dependency (C6, C24, C39-C41), fusion with heminodes (C10, C32, C99), and mobility toward heminodes (C96-C97). While the contribution to node development is strongly supported by fusion observations, the quantitative importance of this pathway versus heminode-only assembly cannot be determined from the data.
